flawed_step: The natural proof is induction on the number of vertices: remove a leaf from each tree, match the smaller trees by the inductive hypothesis, then reattach the leaf. This breaks at the reattachment step. The degree sequence records how many vertices have each degree, not which vertex the leaf hangs from. So the leaf can hang from degree-matched vertices that sit in different places in the two trees, and nothing forces an isomorphism.
counterexample: Take two trees on 6 vertices. T1: edges c-a, a-b, b-d, c-e, c-f (a spider with legs of length 3, 1 and 1). T2: edges c-a, a-d, c-b, b-e, c-f (a spider with legs of length 2, 2 and 1). Both have degree sequence (3,2,2,1,1,1). In T1 the two degree-2 vertices (a and b) are adjacent. In T2 they are not. An isomorphism keeps degrees and adjacency, so these trees are not isomorphic.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The inductive proof fails because the degree sequence does not say where a removed leaf was attached. Two 6-vertex trees with degree sequence (3,2,2,1,1,1) show this. In one tree the two degree-2 vertices are adjacent and in the other they are not, so no isomorphism exists.
